text.p: NURSES AWAIT FATE AT HANDS OF SAUDI COURT
Two British nurses in Saudi Arabia are expected to have to wait at least a week for a court to decide whether they murdered their Australian colleague, Yvonne Gilford.
Lucille McLaughlan and Deborah Parry could be beheaded if they are found guilty.
The final day of the trial in the eastern city of Khobar saw a last-minute presentation of evidence from Australia.
On Friday, a South Australian Supreme Court judge ordered a temporary injunction restraining the brother of murder victim Yvonne Gilford from repeating his calls for the two accused to be executed.
Under Islamic law, the victim's family has the right to spare the lives of convicted killers.
The defence hopes the Australian ruling will help exclude Ms Gilford's family from giving its life or death verdict.
The Saudi court is closed to the media, but a British diplomatic source said it had now finished hearings and was considering its verdict.
No date has been set for a judgement.
COMPANY DENIES FRUSTRATING TALKS ON MINE DISPUTE
Rio Tinto has said it is prepared to hold another month of negotiations with the coal miners' union in a bid to avert further strike action at its Hunter Valley Number One Coal Mine.
Mine manager Allan Davies said the union notified him on Friday it would proceed with a week-long strike tomorrow following a break-down in negotiations over an enterprise agreement.
Mr Davies has denied union claims that Rio Tinto has tried to frustrate the negotiations over the past three weeks.
But Mick Kelly of the miners' union said it was Mr Davies who had walked away from the negotiations.
Commissioner Harrison of the New South Wales Industrial Commission will act as mediator in the talks today and tomorrow.
ISLANDERS AT RISK OF AIDS FROM TRAWLER CREWS'
The Queensland and Federal Governments fear an HIV epidemic in the Torres Strait due to infection from foreign nationals .

Federal Health Minister Michael Wooldridge, who is in Bangkok, has warned that Australia's indigenous population faces a new threat of AIDS infection brought into the Torres Strait by Thai trawler crews.
Queensland Health Minister Mike Horan said he has asked his counterpart for additional funding to deal with the threat as a condition for the state signing the third national HIV/AIDS strategy.
"We do know that in the event of an AIDS epidemic coming through from parts of south-east Asia, that we'd need additional staff," he said.
"We're the frontline health barrier in the event of some of these diseases coming through from south-east Asia.
"I'm certain in the process of signing the HIV/AIDS strategy, the third national strategy, that the Commonwealth now will recognise that."
TEENAGER CELEBRATES JUNIOR ROWING GOLD
Perth teenager Amber Bradley has won a gold medal at the world junior rowing championships in Belgium.
The 17-year-old student from Penrhos College led the entire race to clinch the singles sculls title by a margin of two-and-a-half seconds from a French competitor.
Bradley said she was delighted to discover she came first.
"I was absolutely stoked," she said.
"I didn't know when I crossed the line if I'd won or not. I knew I was up there but I wasn't sure.
"So it was just amazing."
TAX REFORM SET TO DOMINATE CABINET AGENDA
Federal Cabinet is expected to discuss taxation reform today in the wake of last week's High Court ruling that some state taxes are invalid.
The meeting also follows a report from Australian industry calling for major policy change.
The two-day Cabinet meeting coincides with Prime Minister John Howard's first day back at work after being hospitalised with pneumonia.

It is likely to discuss the the High Court's decision which struck down $5 billion worth of State taxes, and a report from the Metal Trades Industry Associaiton which warns 100,000 jobs are at risk unless there is radical change in industry policy.
That report also calls for taxation reform, saying it may well involve the introduction of a goods and services tax.
Ahead of the meeting, two ministers have refused to rule out the possiblity of holding a referendum on the GST.
Meanwhile, Treasury officials from different states are meeting in Sydney today to discuss the Federal Government's changes to taxes on alcohol, petrol and tobacco.
A spokesman for New South Wales Treasurer Michael Egan said the officials needed to work out a uniform system that will be satisfactory to all States.
Following the High Court ruling, the Commonwealth has begun collecting the taxes.
YOUNG AUSTRALIAN BASKETBALLERS WIN GOLD

The Australian under-23 basketball team has proved it is the best youth side in the world. The Crocs won the gold medal at the World Championships at Melbourne Park last night, beating Puerto Rico by 15 points, 88 to 73.
Australia led by eight points at half time, and stretched the lead to 17 points during the second half, thanks to strong offensive plays by Sam Mackinnon and Brendon Mann.
Chris Anstey took to the court for only eight minutes of the match.
He fouled three times in the first half and was fouled off with six minutes of the game to go.
Aaron Trahair top scored for Australia, with 18 points.
Coach Ian Stacker said the win was a true team effort.
"Every player on the team at some stage has some contribution," he said.
"I think it's just a win that takes on Apollo 13 proportions as far as teamwork goes."
BAD WEEKEND ON NSW ROADS
Eleven people have died on New South Wales roads over the weekend.
In the latest accident, three people died and two others were seriously injured when their car hit a power pole at Belfield in Sydney's west last night.
One of the dead, a man, was thrown from the car by the impact, and the others had to be freed from the wreckage by the Fire Brigade.
Five adults and three children were killed in six other accidents in the state.
And in Tasmania, one person died and another was seriously injured in what's believed to have been a single-vehicle accident on the Bass Highway near Launceston last night.
